issues.legal_issue: The Supreme Court may reappraise evidence in a criminal appeal when the interests of justice require examination of a possible miscarriage of justice.
material_facts: The appeals concerned convictions of many accused persons, largely based on eyewitness testimony.
The appellants alleged that the evidence had been incorrectly appreciated, raising a concern that the convictions might reflect a miscarriage of justice.
The Supreme Court examined the evidence itself.
issues.conclusion: Although the Supreme Court ordinarily does not reappraise evidence in its extraordinary appellate jurisdiction, it may do so when the interests of justice require it; it reappraised the evidence in this case.
issues.legal_principle: Under Article 136 of the Constitution, factual conclusions of the High Court are ordinarily treated as final, but that does not bar the Supreme Court from reappraising evidence when the interests of justice demand it.

issues.definition: When a criminal appeal involves many eyewitness-based convictions and a challenge raising possible misappreciation, the evidence may be reappraised if justice requires it.

issues.legal_issue: A discrepancy about where a first report was written and delay in recording witness statements do not, by themselves, require rejection of eyewitness testimony when the evidence is otherwise corroborated and the delay is explained.
material_facts: The High Court found that the first report had not been written at the place of occurrence as claimed by a witness.
Several eyewitnesses were injured during the incident and corroborated the principal witness about the assaults, weapons, victims and arrival of officials.
Witness statements were recorded several days after the incident, after the initial investigating officer was replaced because the investigation was considered unfair.
issues.conclusion: The discrepancy about the report and the delay in recording statements did not justify rejecting the prosecution case; the corroborated eyewitness testimony was accepted.
issues.legal_principle: The credibility of testimony and the effect of delayed examination must be assessed in the circumstances of the case. A discrepancy in the first report does not necessarily invalidate the prosecution case, and an adequately explained delay need not undermine otherwise reliable testimony. The Court applied these principles without citing an earlier case on this issue.

issues.definition: When injured witnesses corroborate an account despite a report-location discrepancy, and delayed statements are explained by an investigation transfer, the corroborated eyewitness testimony is accepted in the credibility challenge.

issues.legal_issue: Participation in an assault does not establish a shared intention to murder when the participants caused only minor, non-vital injuries and the fatal injuries were attributable to other weapons.
material_facts: A group of accused persons was convicted of murder with shared intention for the death of one victim.
The accused whose murder convictions were reduced had used blunt weapons and caused injuries that were not vital.
The victim’s fatal injuries were caused by pointed weapons, and the medical evidence associated the minor injuries with blunt weapons.
The Court found that the evidence did not establish beyond reasonable doubt that those accused shared an intention to murder.
issues.conclusion: The murder convictions of the accused who caused only minor, non-vital injuries were set aside and replaced with convictions for causing grievous hurt with shared intention.
issues.legal_principle: Under Sections 34 and 325 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may form before or during an offence, but it must be inferred from proved circumstances and not merely from similar intentions, presence, weapons, or participation in an assault. The Court relied on Kripal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pandurang, Tukia and Bhillia v. State of Hyderabad, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Hardev Singh v. State of Punjab.

issues.legal_issue: A shared intention to murder may be inferred where participants in a coordinated assault used deadly weapons and the fatal injuries were consistent with that assault.
material_facts: Several accused were convicted of murder with shared intention for the death of a victim who sustained fatal chest injuries and other injuries.
The group included persons who fired guns and persons who used pointed weapons, including spears.
The evidence placed those accused in the coordinated assault, and the medical evidence indicated that pointed weapons could have caused the fatal injuries.
The Court found the murder convictions justified for the accused who fired or used deadly weapons in the assault.
issues.conclusion: The murder convictions with shared intention of the accused who fired or used deadly weapons in the assault were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code applies where common intention is established from the circumstances; it may arise at the scene and need not have been formed beforehand. The nature of the weapons, the parts of the body attacked, the medical evidence and the participants’ conduct may establish that intention. The Court relied on Kripal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pandurang, Tukia and Bhillia v. State of Hyderabad, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Hardev Singh v. State of Punjab.

issues.legal_issue: A shared intention to murder may be inferred from concerted use of deadly weapons where multiple serious and fatal injuries correspond to the participants’ assault.
material_facts: Twelve accused were convicted of murder with shared intention for the death of a victim who had numerous injuries, including fatal injuries to the head, chest and abdomen.
The participants used guns, cutting weapons and pointed weapons, and the medical evidence showed injuries consistent with those weapons.
The Court found that the accused acted in concert and that the injuries and weapons left no room for doubt that they shared an intention to kill, which developed during the incident.
issues.conclusion: The murder convictions with shared intention of all twelve accused for this victim’s death were affirmed.
issues.legal_principle: Under Section 34 of the Indian Penal Code, common intention may be inferred from concerted action and the nature and extent of injuries when the evidence establishes that the participants acted together to cause death. The Court relied on Aher Pitha Vaishi v. State of Gujarat and also considered the principles in Kripal v. State of Uttar Pradesh, Pandurang, Tukia and Bhillia v. State of Hyderabad, Mohan Singh v. State of Punjab, and Hardev Singh v. State of Punjab.

issues.legal_issue: A conviction for rioting may be affirmed when credible eyewitness testimony establishes the accused persons’ participation in an assembly that used force or violence.
material_facts: The appeal challenged convictions for rioting.
The evidence described a large armed group that used force and attacked people at the scene.
Several witnesses, including injured witnesses, identified the participants, and the trial court and High Court accepted their testimony.
The Supreme Court also accepted that testimony when assessing the related appeal.
issues.conclusion: The convictions for rioting and the sentences imposed on the appellants in that appeal were affirmed, and the appeal was dismissed.
issues.legal_principle: Section 147 of the Indian Penal Code concerns rioting. The Court relied on the credible eyewitness evidence, including evidence from injured witnesses, and found no infirmity in the concurrent findings of the trial court and High Court. No earlier case was cited for this ruling.
